title: Overture Divisions Multilingual Gazetteer (Name Index)
description: **EXPERIMENTAL.** The schema of this collection may change without notice, and the Source Cooperative repository that serves it is unlisted. The gazetteer itself -- a search sidecar, not a boundary dataset: 5,604,413 rows over 3,572,796 divisions in 272 countries, sorted by a folded form of the name. 2,031,617 of those rows are alternative spellings drawn from Overture's `names.common` map across 1,012 language codes, each pointing back at its division through `alt_of`, which is what makes this catalog worth its ODbL obligations. It resolves place names and administrative boundaries, **not street addresses**: there is no house number and no interpolation here. **The sort is the whole design.** This index is far too large to load whole, so the intended path is HTTP range requests: row group statistics on `name_norm` are tight, non-overlapping alphabetical ranges, the footer declares the sort, and the Parquet page index is written, so a typed prefix resolves from one or two row groups of about 478 KiB. A client that wants a keystroke answered with no round trip at all loads the **prominent index** instead -- a second, 8.6 MiB file in this same collection, same schema and same sort, holding every division down to localadmin, every alternative-language spelling of every country, and every locality Overture ranks at prominence 50 or above. `names/index.json` describes it under `prominent_index` with its selection criteria in full. Every row of either file carries the GERS `feature_id` that joins it to a boundary collection, a bbox to fly to, a point, and an advisory `geometry_ref` that turns the geometry fetch into a single range read. 2,952,062 divisions, almost all localities, have no polygon anywhere in this catalog and say so through `has_boundary`. The [agent guide](AGENTS.md) has the prefix-lookup recipe and the join back to geometry. **ODbL share-alike applies.** A database derived from this collection has to be released under ODbL as well, and an application that shows it has to display the attribution: *© OpenStreetMap contributors. Available under the [Open Database License](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright).* The [CC-BY-4.0 counterpart](https://source.coop/portolan-mirrors/geoboundaries-catalog) carries no such obligation and less coverage.

table:columns.name: name
table:columns.description: The spelling to display, byte for byte as Overture published it. On a primary row it is `names.primary`; on an alternative row it is the value Overture lists under one language code in `names.common`. Display this; search `name_norm`.

table:columns.name: name_norm
table:columns.description: Derived, and **the column the file is sorted by**. The folding is fixed by the index contract: Unicode NFD, combining marks (category Mn) dropped, everything outside Unicode letters, digits, space, hyphen and apostrophe replaced by a space, whitespace collapsed, trimmed, lowercased. So 'Zurich' finds 'Zürich' and 'koln' finds 'Köln'. A script with no Latin decomposition, such as Han or Arabic, is lowercased and otherwise unchanged, so it is findable only in its own script. The sort is byte-wise on the UTF-8 encoding and not a locale collation, which is what lets a JavaScript `a < b` on the same folded strings agree with the file's order.

table:columns.name: level
table:columns.description: Derived. This catalog's 0-to-4 mapping of Overture's subtype, and the level contract a geocoder filters on: 0 country and dependency, 1 region, 2 county, 3 localadmin, 4 locality. It is **not** Overture's `admin_level`, which is null below county and puts a dependency at 1. The boundary collection that holds a row's geometry is the one at the same level.

table:columns.name: subtype
table:columns.description: Attested. Overture's own placetype, carried through so that the two subtypes sharing level 0 stay distinguishable: `country`, `dependency`, `region`, `county`, `localadmin` or `locality`.

table:columns.name: class
table:columns.description: Attested. Overture's `class` on the division row: how settled a locality is, one of `city`, `town`, `village` or `hamlet`. It is **a ranking signal, not a filter**, and it is null above locality: measured on this release, Overture populates it on 3,394,627 of 3,508,156 localities and on none of the 64,640 divisions above them, so 113,529 localities have no class and some of those are real cities. The distribution is hamlet 1,715,416, village 1,561,816, town 103,175, city 14,220, which makes `class IN ('city', 'town')` 117,395 places out of 3.5 million. It is in this index because ranking verification showed a short prefix is otherwise dominated by alternative-language rows of countries and regions -- Baghdad buried under Tajik and Uzbek spellings of Bahamas -- and no other column separates a city from a country that happens to share a prefix. `area_km2` makes it worse, because a country always dwarfs a city.

table:columns.name: country
table:columns.description: Derived. ISO 3166-1 alpha-3, mapped from Overture's alpha-2 through the official ISO 3166-1 table packaged with pycountry, so this index and the CC-BY counterpart can be filtered with one code system. A country row carries its own code. A synthetic Overture code with no alpha-3 equivalent is carried through unchanged.

table:columns.name: feature_id
table:columns.description: Attested. The GERS id of the **division**, which is `division_id` in every boundary collection. It is a logical key and never a row offset, which is what makes a version skew between this index and the boundary files recoverable rather than silently wrong. An alternative-name row repeats its division's `feature_id`, so a result list dedupes on it.

table:columns.name: source
table:columns.description: Constant `overture-divisions` on every row. The index contract allows one index to hold several sources and requires a result to be able to say where it came from; this index holds one.

table:columns.name: name_lang
table:columns.description: Attested, and **not always a language code**. It is the key Overture uses for this spelling in `names.common`, carried through unchanged. 1,012 distinct keys appear in this index and 965 of them are BCP-47 shaped; the other 47, covering 48,137 rows, are OpenStreetMap annotation keys rather than languages. `genitive` alone accounts for 46,479 of them, and `suffix`, `short`, `note`, `abbr` and `full` make up most of the rest. Those rows are worth indexing, because a user may well type an inflected or abbreviated form, but an interface that prints this column as a language label will print `genitive`. Null on a primary row, where the language of `names.primary` is unstated. Where several keys agree on one spelling the index keeps a single row holding the first key in alphabetical order, with `name_lang_count` saying how many agreed.

table:columns.name: name_lang_count
table:columns.description: Derived. How many of Overture's language codes map to this exact folded spelling for this division. 1 on a primary row. It is high where a name travels unchanged between languages, which is also a usable signal that a spelling is widely recognized.

table:columns.name: alt_of
table:columns.description: Derived. Null on a primary row; on an alternative-name row it holds that row's own `feature_id`, which is the index contract's way of marking the row as an alternative spelling of a division whose primary row is elsewhere in the file. Filter `alt_of IS NULL` for one row per division.

table:columns.name: parent_name
table:columns.description: Derived. `names.primary` of the division's parent, so an autocomplete can show 'Springfield, Illinois' without a second fetch. Null for a country, which has no parent.

table:columns.name: area_km2
table:columns.description: Derived. The division's geodesic land area in square kilometres, copied from its boundary row, as float32 because an index this size cannot afford a double for a relevance weight. **Null where `has_boundary` is false**, which is most localities. Of two divisions with the same name, the larger is usually the one meant.

table:columns.name: population
table:columns.description: Attested. Overture's `population` for the division where it has one, carried byte for byte. Undated, and **sparse in a way a ranker has to handle explicitly**: measured on this release, Overture populates it on 79.9% of countries (175 of 219), 30.6% of regions, 21.3% of counties, 35.0% of localadmins and 17.7% of localities (621,090 of 3,508,156). Null means unknown, never zero -- a client that coalesces it to 0 sorts every unpopulated place last, which at level 4 is five rows in six. Use it as a relevance weight alongside `prominence` and `class`, not as a census figure.

table:columns.name: prominence
table:columns.description: Attested. Overture's `cartography.prominence`, its own ranking of how important a place is to show on a map. Documented as cartographic guidance rather than a measurement, so use it as a tie-break.

table:columns.name: name_dupes
table:columns.description: Derived. How many rows of this index share this row's `name_norm`, counted worldwide and across levels and across primary and alternative rows. An autocomplete needs it to decide when to disambiguate: the most repeated folded name in this index occurs 1,019 times.

table:columns.name: has_boundary
table:columns.description: Derived. True when a boundary collection in this catalog holds a polygon for this division. False on 2,952,062 of the 3,572,796 primary rows, all of them localities that Overture publishes as a point only. On a false row `bbox` is the division's point collapsed to zero width, `area_km2` is null and `geometry_ref` is null, so a client knows before it fetches that there is no outline to draw.

table:columns.name: bbox
table:columns.description: The extent to fly a map to after a hit, as xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax. It is the division's full extent where a boundary exists and the division's point, collapsed, where one does not. Stored as **float32 with every bound rounded outward**, which halves what four coordinates a row cost across millions of rows; the box therefore always contains the division but is approximate to about 1e-5 degrees, roughly a metre. The boundary collections keep float64. A signed box where xmin > xmax would mean an antimeridian crossing.

table:columns.name: geometry_ref
table:columns.description: Derived, and **advisory**. `file`, `row_group` and `row`: where this division's geometry sits in its boundary collection, and at the same index in that collection's display companion, which holds the same rows in the same groups. It turns a geometry fetch into one range read with no search. A consumer must still verify that the `division_id` it decodes equals `feature_id` and fall back to a lookup on mismatch, because this is a hint and the catalog version is what makes it valid. Null on an alternative-name row and on a point-only division.

table:columns.name: geometry
table:columns.description: Derived. A Point as WKB in CRS84: `ST_PointOnSurface` of the division's land polygon where there is one, which is guaranteed to fall inside the division where a centroid is not, and Overture's own division point where there is not. Use it for a marker, never as the division's geometry. **Null on an alternative-name row**, which describes the same division as its primary row; repeating the point on two million alternative rows cost 40 MB and said nothing new.

data.title: Multilingual name index, GeoParquet 1.1 (876 row groups of 6,400 rows, zstd, page index, sorted by name_norm)
data.description: The whole gazetteer. Too large to load in a browser, and not meant to be: it is sorted by `name_norm` so a typed prefix is a range request. A client that wants an answer with no round trip loads the `prominent-index` asset instead and comes here for anything that file can miss.

prominent-index.title: Prominent gazetteer index, GeoParquet 1.1 (71 row groups of 1,536 rows, 8.6 MiB, same schema and sort as the full index)
prominent-index.description: A strict row subset of the full index -- 108,919 rows of 5,604,413 -- small enough for a client to fetch whole on focus and answer keystrokes from memory, while the full index stays available by range request for anything deeper. Same schema, same sort, same `feature_id` and `geometry_ref`, so a hit found here resolves its geometry exactly as a hit found there. It holds every division from country down to localadmin, every alternative-language spelling of every country and dependency, and every locality Overture ranks at `cartography.prominence` 50 or above. What it can miss, and therefore when to fall back: any locality below that cut, and any alternative-language name of a region, county, localadmin or locality. The full criteria, with row counts per level, are in `index.json` under `prominent_index.criteria`.

index-manifest.title: Gazetteer manifest for the geocoder (cnmw-index/1.0)
index-manifest.description: The few kilobytes a client fetches before anything else. For the full index, the prominent index and every boundary and display file: the URL, size, checksum, row count, row group count and `row_group_rows`, plus two exact metadata sizes. `footer_bytes` is the whole trailing span, thrift footer plus page index, so one range request of exactly that many bytes from the end of a file leaves a client holding all of its metadata; `footer_metadata_bytes` is the thrift footer alone, the minimum needed to locate row groups and what a hyparquet client should pass as `initialFetchSize`. Without them hyparquet speculates a 512 KiB tail, which on the 409 MB index is a guaranteed second round trip because its footer is 2.1 MB. Also carries `prominent_index.criteria` -- exactly which rows the small index holds and what it can miss -- the catalog version, and the attribution each file requires with a share_alike flag.

upstream-division-s3.title: Overture release 2026-10-21.0, type=division, on S3 over HTTPS (1 file, 0.58 GB)
upstream-division-s3.description: Every division record in the release: the names, the hierarchy and a point per division. The names collection here is built from this type, and every collection takes its names from it. The same bytes are addressable as `s3://overturemaps-us-west-2/release/2026-10-21.0/theme=divisions/type=division/` for DuckDB, GDAL and the AWS CLI; the bucket is public and anonymous and the requester does not pay. Measured 2026-11-12, this HTTPS endpoint answers `Accept-Ranges: bytes` and sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with `Content-Range` and `Accept-Ranges` exposed, so a browser can range-read it cross-origin. This is the authoritative release, not a copy of it: use it for bulk download, for analysis over the whole theme, and for anything where the answer has to come from Overture rather than from a mirror. It is not what this catalog's files are for, and the difference is layout rather than reachability -- measured 2026-11-12 on part-00000 of type=division: 4,700,999 rows in 256 row groups of about 18,400 rows, median 2.22 MB and up to 3.85 MB compressed per row group, 50 leaf column chunks, no declared sort, and a 1.47 MB footer that takes a reader two requests because a speculative 512 KiB tail falls short. Finding one place by name in it means scanning every part file; pulling one division's geometry means fetching a multi-megabyte row group of the full 50-column schema. The files in this catalog are the same data sorted, projected and laid out so that each of those is one small range request. See the catalog README's "The upstream data vs our optimized files".

upstream-division-area-s3.description: The polygons. Every boundary collection in this catalog is a projection of one `subtype` of this type, joined to type=division for names. upstream-divisions-azure.title: Overture release 2026-10-21.0, divisions theme, on the Azure Blob mirror
upstream-divisions-azure.description: Overture publishes every release to Azure Blob Storage as well as to S3, and these are the same files under `type=division/` and `type=division_area/`. **It sends no CORS headers**, measured 2026-11-12, so unlike the S3 HTTPS endpoint it cannot be read from a browser cross-origin; it is for server-side and CLI consumers, and for anyone whose egress is cheaper from Azure. This is the authoritative release, not a copy of it: use it for bulk download, for analysis over the whole theme, and for anything where the answer has to come from Overture rather than from a mirror.
